questions.q: How do I fix a typo in my registration?
questions.a: Contact your county election office (https://www.sos.mn.gov/elections-voting/find-county-election-office/).

questions.q: How do I get a copy of my voter registration card or proof of registration?
questions.a: Minnesota does not issue voter registration cards. If you need proof of voter registration you can contact your county election office (https://www.sos.mn.gov/elections-voting/find-county-election-office/).

questions.q: How do I change my party registration?
questions.a:
Voters do not declare a party when they register to vote in Minnesota, so there is nothing to change! Minnesota has an "open primary" so voters choose which party's primary to participate in when they vote their ballot.

In most cases no one will know which party's primary you voted in. However, for the Presidential Primary (https://www.sos.mn.gov/elections-voting/how-elections-work/presidential-primary/), the major party chair will get a list of voters who chose their party's ballot.

questions.q: How do I cancel my registration?
questions.a: Complete the Request to Inactivate Voter Record (https://www.sos.mn.gov/media/2244/request-to-inactivate-voter-record.pdf), and send it to your county election office (https://www.sos.mn.gov/elections-voting/find-county-election-office/).

questions.q: How do I let someone know a voter has died?
questions.a: Minnesota election officials get death reports daily from the Minnesota Department of Health and Social Security Administration, so voters that die will be removed from the registration rolls through that process. If you would like to notify election officials separately, you can send the Report of Deceased Voter (https://www.sos.mn.gov/media/3fpjg21m/report-of-deceased-voter-form.pdf) form to the county election official (https://www.sos.mn.gov/elections-voting/find-county-election-office/).

questions.q: What voter data is public and private?
questions.a:
A registered voter's name, address, year of birth, and phone number (if given by the voter) is public data. Which elections someone voted in is also public, but how a voter marked their individual ballot is never recorded--ballots are always secret.

Although the data above is public, it is not available to anyone who asks for any purpose--it is restricted to certain people for specific uses. The registered voter list (https://www.sos.mn.gov/election-administration-campaigns/data-maps/registered-voter-list-requests/) webpage has details about these restrictions as well as ordering information. See the Data Practices Policy for Data Subjects (https://www.sos.mn.gov/media/pkbiiqpv/data-practices-policy-for-data-subjects-2025.pdf) to get information on your own voter record.

Read the privacy notice for voter registration applications (https://www.sos.mn.gov/elections-voting/register-to-vote/privacy-notice-for-voter-registration-applications/) to learn what data is kept private and why private data is collected, or the following question if you have concerns about your privacy.

questions.q: What if I have safety or privacy concerns?
questions.a:
Your name and address are public when you register to vote. However, if you have safety or privacy concerns, there are ways to register and vote without making your information public:

1. Safe at Home address confidentiality program
2. Request your address be withheld from the public voter list
3. Inactivate your voter record and reregister later

More details about these three options are on the I fear for my personal safety (https://www.sos.mn.gov/elections-voting/register-to-vote/i-fear-for-my-personal-safety/) webpage.

questions.q: How do I register close to Election Day?
questions.a:
Unlike many states, you can wait until Election Day to register in Minnesota. However, we encourage you to register before Election Day—it will save you time at the polling place.

- The deadline to register online is 11:59 p.m. 21 days before Election Day.
- The deadline to register on paper is 5 p.m. 21 days before Election Day.
- Within 20 days before the election, you can submit a registration form but it will not be processed until after Election Day.
- You can always register when you vote, either at a polling place, or when voting absentee.

questions.q: How do I vote if I'm moving close to Election Day?
questions.a:
If you moved to Minnesota later than 21 days before an election, you will not have time to establish residence in Minnesota for voting. If you are moving within Minnesota before an election, you will want to register and vote at the address you will be living at on Election Day.

If you're moving from Minnesota, you will need to consult the voting laws of the state you are moving to. If you move from Minnesota within 30 days before a presidential election to a state you are not eligible to register in, you can apply to vote for U.S. president (https://www.sos.mn.gov/elections-voting/register-to-vote/common-registration-questions/) in Minnesota.

Other questions? Contact your county election office (https://www.sos.mn.gov/elections-voting/find-county-election-office/) or call the Secretary of State at 1-877-600-VOTE (8683).

questions.q: Who can vote?
questions.a:
To vote in Minnesota, you must be a U.S. citizen, at least 18 years old on Election Day, and a resident of Minnesota for at least 20 days. If you had a felony conviction, you can vote if you are not currently incarcerated, even if you are on probation or parole.

Paying out-of-state tuition or having a driver's license from another state does not necessarily mean you can't vote in Minnesota.

questions.q: What is my voting residence?
questions.a:
You should register to vote from the address you currently consider home. For many students, this is likely a school address or a parent’s house. If you still go back to visit but no longer consider it your home, then you should register to vote where you live at school.

If you moved to Minnesota from another state and currently consider Minnesota your home, you can vote here even if you pay out-of-state tuition or have a driver’s license from another state.

If you do not consider your school address to be your home, you can apply to vote by mail with an absentee ballot.

Minnesota voters can apply online (https://www.sos.mn.gov/elections-voting/other-ways-to-vote/vote-early-by-mail/); otherwise, visit your home state’s election website.

questions.q: How do I register to vote?
questions.a:
You must be registered to vote at your current address. It is best to register before Election Day (https://www.sos.mn.gov/elections-voting/register-to-vote/register-online/), but it is not required. To register on Election Day, you must show proof of your name and current address (https://www.sos.mn.gov/elections-voting/register-to-vote/register-on-election-day/). If you don't have ID or bill with your current address, college students are able to use a photo ID along with their name and address on a student housing list from the college as proof of residence.

Colleges and universities that enroll students accepting state financial aid must send election officials a student housing list. This list includes students who live on-campus and those that have provided their current address to the school and live in the city where campus is located. If you are on the list, show any form of photo ID approved for registering on election day (https://www.sos.mn.gov/elections-voting/register-to-vote/register-on-election-day/) to complete your registration.

questions.q: What's on my ballot?
questions.a: See the candidates and questions (https://www.sos.mn.gov/elections-voting/whats-on-my-ballot/get-a-sample-ballot/) that will be on your ballot.

questions.q: Where do I vote?
questions.a: Find out where you vote (https://www.sos.mn.gov/elections-voting/election-day-voting/where-do-i-vote/). Most polling places are open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m.

questions.q: Do I need to bring ID?
questions.a:
If your voter registration is current and active, you do not need to bring identification. This means you were successfully registered at least 21 days before Election Day and you have not moved or changed names since then.

If you need to register or update your registration, or you have not voted in four years or more, you will need to show proof of residence (https://www.sos.mn.gov/elections-voting/register-to-vote/register-on-election-day/) before you vote.

questions.q: How does automatic voter registration work?
questions.a:
Automatic voter registration is called automatic because of its convenience for applicants. In fact, the process of registering someone to vote under this new law is complex and involves multiple points of human verification.

The process begins when a customer applies for a permit, driver’s license, or identification card. During the transaction, the applicant provides the required documentation to DVS. If the applicant provides citizenship-affirming documentation, DVS sends the applicant’s information to the Office of the Minnesota Secretary of State for voter registration. If the applicant does not provide citizenship-affirming documentation, DVS does not send their information for voter registration. After receiving the information from DVS, state election officials conduct an additional review to verify that the applicant’s right to vote has not been revoked by a court. If the applicant is confirmed as eligible, their information is provided to their county election office for voter registration.

Applicants will be mailed an opt-out notice (https://www.sos.mn.gov/media/5800/automatic-voter-registration-sample-notice.pdf) to their residence. If the opt-out is returned within 20 days, then the applicant will not be registered. If the opt-out notice is not returned, the voter will be registered to vote.

The opt-out notice is available in:

- Spanish  (https://www.sos.mn.gov/media/5858/avr-opt-out-letter_spanish.pdf)- Español
- Somali  (https://www.sos.mn.gov/media/5857/avr-opt-out-letter_somali.pdf)- Soomaali
- Hmong  (https://www.sos.mn.gov/media/5860/avr-opt-out-letter_hmong.pdf)- Hmoob
- Amharic  (https://www.sos.mn.gov/media/5846/avr-opt-out-letter-_amharic.pdf)- አማርኛ
- Khmer  (https://www.sos.mn.gov/media/5848/avr-opt-out-letter_khmer.pdf)- ខ្មែរ
- Lao  (https://www.sos.mn.gov/media/5849/avr-opt-out-letter_lao.pdf)- ພາສາລາວ
- Oromo  (https://www.sos.mn.gov/media/5850/avr-opt-out-letter_oromo.pdf)- Afaan Oromo
- Russian  (https://www.sos.mn.gov/media/5856/avr-opt-out-letter_russian.pdf)- Pусский
- Chinese  (https://www.sos.mn.gov/media/5852/avr-opt-out-letter_simpchinese.pdf)- 中文
- Vietnamese  (https://www.sos.mn.gov/media/5859/avr-opt-out-letter_vietnamese.pdf)- Tiếng Việt

questions.q: When will I be registered to vote?
questions.a:
Since there is a 20-day opt-out period and a verification process, voter registration may take 4-6 weeks from when a person first applies for their state-issued ID. Minnesotans can check their voter registration (https://www.sos.mn.gov/elections-voting/register-to-vote/check-your-registration/) status online.

Once a person is registered to vote, a postcard will be mailed to their address with their polling place location, precincts, and election districts. If the postal verification card is unable to be delivered by the U.S. Postal Service, their voter record will be challenged. A second postal verification card is sent and if that card cannot be delivered their voter record will be inactivated.

questions.q: What if I do not want to register to vote?
questions.a: Once eligibility has been verified, and the county election office has processed the application, a notification will be mailed to the applicant. The notice will include information on how to opt-out if the person does not wish to register to vote. If the opt-out notice is returned within 20 days, they will not be registered to vote. Additionally, when registered, voters may request to inactivate their voter record (https://www.sos.mn.gov/media/2244/request-to-inactivate-voter-record.pdf) at any time.

questions.q: Who is eligible for automatic voter registration?
questions.a:
Only individuals who present citizenship documentation, such as a U.S. birth certificate or U.S. passport, will be registered to vote.

Eligible 16- and 17-year-olds will be pre-registered to vote and will be automatically registered to vote when they turn 18.

In Minnesota, you are eligible to register to vote if you:

- Are at least 16 years old to pre-register and at least 18 years old on the day of the election in which you intend to vote
- Are a U.S. citizen
- Maintain residence in Minnesota for at least 20 days before Election Day
- Are not currently incarcerated for a felony conviction
- Are not under court-ordered guardianship in which the court order revokes your right to vote
- Have not been found by a court to be legally incompetent to vote

questions.q: What if I am already registered to vote?
questions.a:
If you apply for or renew your license or ID card with Driver and Vehicle Services, and the data provided matches the name and address associated with your voter record, no action will be taken.

If your name and/or address have changed, that information will be provided to your county election office to update your voter record. You will not receive the automatic voter registration notice as you are already registered to vote. However, if your address has changed, you will receive a postcard listing your updated address, along with your polling place location, precincts, and election districts.

Data on Qualifying Transactions and Records Transferred for Registration or Updates to Registrations

The commissioner of public safety must submit monthly data to the secretary of state identifying the total number of individuals who completed qualifying transactions under this section and the total number of individuals whose records were ultimately transferred for registration or updates to registrations. A qualifying transaction occurs when a customer at a DVS service center applies for or renews a Minnesota ID card and presents citizenship-affirming documentation, such as a United States passport.

The Secretary of State must publish a monthly report of this data. Note that this is not the number of individuals who are ultimately registered to vote. Records must first undergo review to determine if there is already an existing voter record and to review whether the applicant’s right to vote has been removed by a court, making them ineligible to vote. See the flowchart of the Automatic Voter Registration process (https://www.sos.mn.gov/media/5845/automatic-voter-registration-flowchart.pdf) for additional information.

questions.q: What is a residential facility?
questions.a:
Residential facilities include:

- Adult foster care programs
- Assisted-living facilities
- Battered women’s shelters
- Homeless shelters
- Housing support settings
- Nursing homes
- Residential alcohol and chemical treatment programs
- Residential facilities for persons with developmental disabilities
- Residential facilities for treatment of mental illness
- Supervised-living facilities
- Transitional housing
- Veterans’ homes

questions.q: Not sure about your legal status?
questions.a: Sometimes it is not clear whether a felony charge results in a felony conviction. If you are unsure, you may want to seek legal advice from an attorney.

questions.q: WHO IS ELIGIBLE TO VOTE ABSENTEE?
questions.a:
In Minnesota, all voters can apply to vote absentee. You do not need to be registered to vote to request an absentee ballot. A voter registration application will be included in the materials.

You must show your witness an accepted proof of residence (https://www.sos.state.mn.us/elections-voting/register-to-vote/register-on-election-day/) when registering.

questions.q: HOW DO I REQUEST AN ABSENTEE BALLOT?
questions.a:
To apply, you will need an email address and your ID number: a Minnesota driver's license or ID card or last 4 digits of Social Security number.

There are multiple ways to request an absentee ballot:

- For Federal, State, or County Elections: Apply online (https://mnvotes.sos.mn.gov/abrequest/index) for an absentee ballot
- For City, Town or School District Elections: Send a completed absentee ballot application (https://www.sos.mn.gov/media/2444/english-regular-absentee-ballot-application.pdf) to your local city, town or school clerk
- Permanent Absentee Voter List: Update your voter registration (https://mnvotes.sos.mn.gov/voterregistration/index/) to become a permanent absentee voter.

If you are a participant in Minnesota's Safe at Home Address Confidentiality Program, contact Safe at Home at 1-866-723-3035 to apply for an absentee ballot.

questions.q: WHAT IS THE DEADLINE TO REQUEST AN ABSENTEE BALLOT?
questions.a: The last day to request an absentee ballot (https://mnvotes.sos.mn.gov/abrequest/index) is 1 day before the election.

questions.q: DO I HAVE TO REQUEST AN ABSENTEE BALLOT EVERY YEAR?
questions.a: You can either apply each year for an absentee ballot, or you can sign up for the permanent absentee voter list by updating your voter registration. (https://mnvotes.sos.mn.gov/voterregistration/index/)

questions.q: WHAT IS THE DEADLINE FOR SUBMITTING AN ABSENTEE BALLOT?
questions.a: Your voted absentee ballot must be received by Election Day to be counted.

questions.q: WHEN ARE ABSENTEE BALLOTS MAILED OUT TO VOTERS WHO HAVE REQUESTED THEM?
questions.a:
Your absentee ballot will be sent to you at least 46 days before the election. If you apply after this date, your ballot will be sent when the application is received.

The only exception is town elections held in March: absentee ballots will be sent 30 days before the election.

questions.q: HOW DO I COMPLETE MY ABSENTEE BALLOT?
questions.a:
1. Read the instructions that come with your ballot carefully.
2. You will need a witness when you vote and complete your ballot. The witness can be either a US citizen at least 18 years old on election day or a notary.
3. Return the ballot and forms right away after you finish. Your ballot will not count if it is received after Election Day.

questions.q: HOW DO I RETURN MY VOTED ABSENTEE BALLOT?
questions.a: You have multiple options to return your ballot: you can mail it, deposit it in a secure drop box, use a package delivery service like Fed Ex or UPS, or return your ballot in person at your local elections office (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm).

questions.q: CAN I TRACK MY MAILED ABSENTEE BALLOT?
questions.a: You can sign up to track your absentee ballot (https://mnvotes.sos.mn.gov/abstatus/index) on your Secretary of State website.

questions.q: WHAT IF I REQUESTED AN ABSENTEE BALLOT BUT WANT TO VOTE IN PERSON?
questions.a:
If you requested an absentee ballot, you have the option to vote in person if you have not returned your absentee ballot. You can go to your early voting location before Election Day or your polling place on Election Day.

You should tell the election officials that you requested an absentee ballot but want to vote in person instead. The election official will cancel your absentee ballot and allow you to vote in person. You should shred your absentee ballot when you return home; no other voter may use it.

questions.q: HOW DO I REQUEST AN ABSENTEE BALLOT AS AN OVERSEAS OR US MILITARY VOTER?
questions.a:
Overseas citizens and U.S. military personnel can find information on how to register to vote and request an absentee ballot at the Overseas Vote Foundation. (https://www.overseasvotefoundation.org/vote/home.htm)

  Request your Ballot  (https://mnvotes.sos.state.mn.us/ABRegistration/ABRegistrationStep1.aspx)

questions.q: Does Minnesota allow ballot curing?
questions.a:
If there are fewer than five days before Election Day, election officials will try to contact you. In this case, you can vote in person at your local election office or at your polling place on Election Day.

If you did not fill out the signature envelope correctly, election officials will mail you replacement materials, including an explanation for why your signature envelope was rejected.

Minnesota doesn’t have a ballot curing process for absentee/mail ballots or provisional ballots after Election Day.

questions.q: Can I track my absentee ballot?
questions.a: You can track the status of your absentee/mail ballot using your state’s online tool (https://mnvotes.sos.mn.gov/abstatus/index).

questions.q: What is a ballot drop box?
questions.a: A drop box is a secure, locked structure operated by election officials where voters can deliver their absentee ballot any time, day or night.

questions.q: Are drop boxes available in my state?
questions.a: Yes, vote-by-mail drop boxes are available in Minnesota.

questions.q: Where can I find ballot drop box locations?
questions.a: Some local election officials are using drop boxes. Staffed drop boxes can be used to drop off a voter's own ballot, as well as up to three other voters' ballots if they bring an ID. Unstaffed drop boxes can only be used to drop off a voter's own ballot. To determine what kind of drop boxes are in a voter's area and where they are located, voters should contact their local election office (https://nam10.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.sos.state.mn.us%2Felections-voting%2Ffind-county-election-office%2F&data=04%7C01%7C%7C8c24bf25265d4696c0ba08d86fb33a3b%7C90befbfe6dce4edfba8a35fb67131124%7C0%7C1%7C637382162849700111%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJWIjoiMC4wLjAwMDAiLCJQIjoiV2luMzIiLCJBTiI6Ik1haWwiLCJXVCI6Mn0%3D%7C1000&sdata=EUCdjpBESpk%2FTQtEVg6F7QzMa1WL4mPv04MAC2Qmfys%3D&reserved=0).

questions.q: Can I track the ballot after placing in the drop box?
questions.a: Yes, you can track your ballot by looking up your on the Secretary of State website (https://mnvotes.sos.mn.gov/abstatus/index).

questions.q: Can I vote before Election Day in Minnesota?
questions.a: Yes. Minnesota allows early voting through absentee voting. You can vote before Election Day either by mail or in person at an early voting location.

questions.q: Who can vote early in Minnesota?
questions.a:
Any eligible Minnesota voter can vote early. You do not need a reason or excuse to vote before Election Day.

To vote by mail, you must request an absentee ballot [link to absentee state topic]. You can apply online, by mail, or in person through your local election office. (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm)

questions.q: When can I vote early in Minnesota?
questions.a: Early voting begins 46 days before Election Day in Minnesota. In-person early voting is typically available during regular business hours, with expanded hours in the days leading up to the election. Some local election offices may offer additional days or hours for absentee voting. Contact your local election office (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm) for more information.

questions.q: Where can I vote early in Minnesota?
questions.a: You can vote early in person at your county election office, city clerk’s office, or other designated early voting locations. Locations and hours may vary by area, so check with your local election office (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm) for details.

questions.q: Who is eligible to vote in Minnesota?
questions.a:
You can vote in Minnesota if you:

- Are a U.S. citizen
- Are at least 18 years old by Election Day (you can pre-register at 16 or 17)
- Have lived in Minnesota for at least 20 days before the election
- Are not currently incarcerated for a felony conviction
- Are not under a court order that revokes your right to vote

questions.q: Can I vote in Minnesota if I have a felony conviction?
questions.a: Your criminal record does not affect your right to vote in Minnesota unless you are currently incarcerated for a felony conviction. Your voting rights are not restricted by pretrial detention, misdemeanors, probation, or parole.

questions.q: How do I vote in Minnesota if I don’t have a permanent address?
questions.a:
You can still register and vote in Minnesota without a permanent address. You can use the place where you usually sleep, such as a shelter, a friend’s home, or an outdoor location, as your address.

If you do not have documents showing your address, another registered voter from your precinct or a shelter staff member can confirm where you live when you register or vote.

questions.q: Can students vote in Minnesota?
questions.a:
Yes. Students can register and vote in Minnesota if they meet eligibility requirements. Students should register at the address they consider their primary home, which can be either their school address or their home address.

If you are a student from out of state, you can also choose to vote in your home state using an absentee ballot, but you’ll need to follow your home state’s rules and deadlines. You can find the rules for your state on VOTE411 or by contacting your state’s election office (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm).

questions.q: AM I REQUIRED TO SHOW ID TO REGISTER TO VOTE IN MINNESOTA?
questions.a: It depends on how and when you register. If you register online or by mail, you’ll need to provide your Minnesota driver’s license or state ID number, or the last four digits of your Social Security number. If you register in person on Election Day or during early voting, you must provide an accepted form of proof of residence.

questions.q: WHAT TYPES OF ID CAN I USE TO REGISTER TO VOTE IN MINNESOTA?
questions.a:
To register online or by mail, you’ll need either your Minnesota driver’s license or state ID number. If you don’t have one, you can use the last four digits of your Social Security number.

If you're registering in person on Election Day or during early voting, you have several options:

- A valid Minnesota driver’s license, state ID, or learner’s permit
- A Tribal ID that includes your name, photo, address, and signature
- A student photo ID if your college has submitted a student housing list
- A registered voter from your precinct or a staff person from a residential facility who can confirm your address
- A Notice of Late Registration sent to you by election officials
- Proof that you’re already registered in the same precinct under a different name or address
- A photo ID (which can be expired) plus a bill or document with your name and current address (like a utility bill, bank statement, or lease)

You only need one of these options to register in person.

questions.q: WHAT IF I DON’T HAVE THE REQUIRED ID WHEN I REGISTER IN MINNESOTA?
questions.a:
If you register online or by mail and don’t have a Minnesota ID or a Social Security number, you must write “NONE” in the required field of your application. For in-person registration, if you don’t have documents showing your address, a registered voter from your precinct or a staff person from a residential facility can vouch for you by signing an oath at your polling place.

Voters can call or text 844-338-8743 at any time to reach VoteRiders Voter ID Helpline

questions.q: When are official election results available in Minnesota?
questions.a: Official results are never available on Election Day. Election officials are working around the clock to count a large number of ballots, and it’s essential that they take the time to make sure every vote is counted.

questions.q: Where can I find official election results?
questions.a:
Official election results will be uploaded on Minnesota’s Secretary of State website (https://www.sos.mn.gov/elections-voting/election-results) as they become available. For more information on how Minnesota is ensuring secure and fair elections, visit the state's resource page (https://www.sos.state.mn.us/elections-voting/secure-and-fair-elections/).

  Official Results  (https://www.sos.state.mn.us/elections-voting/election-results)

questions.q: What does a poll worker do in Minnesota?
questions.a:
Poll workers, also called election judges in Minnesota, are trained workers who help run elections at polling places.

They may:

- Set up and close the polling place
- Check in and register voters
- Issue and collect ballots
- Help voters use voting equipment
- Count ballots and certify results

questions.q: What qualifications do I need to be a poll worker in Minnesota?
questions.a:
To be a poll worker in Minnesota, you must:

- Be eligible to vote in Minnesota
- Be able to read, write, and speak English
- Not be a candidate or closely related to a candidate on the ballot in that precinct

Students ages 16 and 17 can serve as trainee poll workers with permission and training.

questions.q: Are poll workers paid in Minnesota?
questions.a: Yes. Poll workers and student trainees are paid for their time, including training and Election Day work. Pay rates vary by location and position. For more information, please reach out to your local elections officials. (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm)

questions.q: How do I apply to be a poll worker in Minnesota?
questions.a: To apply, contact your local city or county election office (https://www.sos.mn.gov/elections-voting/get-involved/become-an-election-judge/). You can also complete an election judge interest form (https://www.sos.mn.gov/media/3110/election-judge-interest-form.pdf) and submit it to your county.

questions.q: What is a provisional ballot?
questions.a: Provisional ballots ensure that all voters can cast a ballot even if voter eligibility isn’t certain when they vote. Voters can mark a provisional ballot, and election workers set it aside until eligibility is verified at a later time.

questions.q: Does Minnesota offer provisional voting?
questions.a: No, there is no provisional voting in Minnesota. Election Day (same-day) registration is available.

questions.q: What voting assistance is available for voters with disabilities?
questions.a:
The Help America Vote Act requires that election authorities have voting equipment for voters with disabilities to vote privately and independently, and Minnesota is no exception.

All polling places should be fully accessible with clearly marked accessible doors and parking spaces. If you cannot easily leave your car, you can ask for the ballot to be brought out to you. If you are unable to go to the polling place due to an illness or disability, you can vote by absentee ballot.

If you have limited vision, you may ask for voter registration and absentee ballot instructions in an alternative format. If you are hearing impaired, every county and most cities will have a TDD device for questions. Materials can be provided in braille, on audio tape, on CD or in large print. To order any brochures or to order a voter registration application and instructions on how to fill it out, contact the secretary of state's elections division (https://www.sos.state.mn.us/elections-voting/election-day-voting/get-help-voting/) at 651-215-1440 or toll free, at 1-877-600-8683. TTY: 1-800-627-3529.

If you need assistance completing the election materials, you may bring a family member, friend, neighbor or anyone you choose to help you vote. You may NOT bring your employer, your union, or a candidate for office to help you vote.

For more information on the provisions available for disabled voters, please contact your local election authority (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm).

questions.q: How do I request accommodation or report accessibility issues?
questions.a: If you have any questions about receiving help in voting, please ask the clerk or inspector at the polling place.

questions.q: Can I vote by mail because of my disability?
questions.a:
Vote-by-mail (absentee voting) is available in Minnesota and no excuse is required. You can find more about how to vote by mail here. (https://www.vote411.org/minnesota#absentee-ballot-process)

For more information, you can utilize the American Association of People With Disabilities (AAPD) (http://www.aapd.com/what-we-do/voting/) resource.

questions.q: What do I need to register to vote in Minnesota?
questions.a:
Here is what you need to know to register in Minnesota:

There are three methods of voter registration in Minnesota: register in-person, register online (https://mnvotes.sos.state.mn.us/VoterRegistration/VoterRegistrationMain.aspx), or mail a printable application (https://www.sos.state.mn.us/elections-voting/register-to-vote/register-on-paper/) to your local elections office.

questions.q: Can I register to vote using my college address in Minnesota?
questions.a: Yes, if you consider your campus address your residence, you can register to vote there. If you move to a different dorm or off campus, be sure to update your voter registration with your new address so you vote in the correct district.

questions.q: What’s the deadline to register to vote in Minnesota?
questions.a: In Minnesota, you must register online or by mail at least 21 days before Election Day. You can also register in person on Election Day, though early registration is encouraged.

questions.q: What form of ID do I need to vote in Minnesota?
questions.a: A Minnesota voter is not required to show identification. However, if you are voting for the first time, you may be asked to show a form of identification when you go to the polls. This can include a driver’s license, passport, student ID from a state-supported college, or other accepted forms.

questions.q: I’m originally from another state, can I still vote in my home state while studying in Minnesota?
questions.a: Yes, you can vote in your home state using an absentee ballot, but you'll need to follow your home state's rules and deadlines. You can find the rules for your state on VOTE411 or by contacting your state’s election office (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm?_ga=2.80770708.201004602.1748545947-889989650.1701105430).

questions.q: Does registering to vote affect my financial aid, parents’ taxes, and/or tuition in Minnesota?
questions.a: Registering to vote in your college community will not affect your Federal Financial Aid, status as a dependent on your parents’ taxes, or tuition status.

questions.q: Does Minnesota require employers to give time off to vote?
questions.a:
Yes. Minnesota law requires employers to give employees time off to vote.

Employees have the right to take time off from work to vote without losing pay, vacation time, or personal leave. You can take the time needed to go to your polling place, vote, and return to work, and your employer cannot penalize you for doing so.

You can share a letter from the Secretary of State (https://www.sos.mn.gov/media/ttbmgvob/letter-to-employers.pdf) with your employer that explains your right to take time off to vote.

questions.q: Do I need an ID to vote in Minnesota?
questions.a: You only need to show ID if you need to register or update your registration at the polls. If you're already registered and your name and address haven't changed, you do not need to show ID to vote.

questions.q: What types of ID can I use to vote in-person in Minnesota?
questions.a:
If you need to register or update your registration at the polling place, you’ll need to show proof of residence. You can do this with:

- A valid Minnesota driver’s license, state ID, or learner’s permit
- A Tribal ID with your name, photo, address, and signature
- A student photo ID if your college provides a housing list to election officials
- A registered voter or staff person from a residential facility who can vouch for your address
- A Notice of Late Registration from election officials
- Proof you’re already registered in the same precinct under a different name or address
- A photo ID (can be expired) plus a current bill with your name and address (such as a utility bill, lease, or bank statement)

questions.q: Does mail/absentee voting require ID?
questions.a:
Usually, no. If your identity was verified when you registered to vote, you do not need to show ID to vote absentee.

When requesting an absentee ballot online, you may be asked to provide your Minnesota driver’s license or state ID number, or the last four digits of your Social Security number.

Some first-time voters or voters registering while voting early (absentee) may need to provide ID or proof of residence.

questions.q: What if I don’t have an acceptable ID?
questions.a: If you are registered under your current name and address, no ID is required. However, if you need to register at the polls and don’t have an accepted ID or document, you'll have to show proof of residence using an approved method (such as having a registered voter vouch for you) before you can vote.

questions.q: Can I use my student ID to vote in Minnesota?
questions.a:
Yes. A student ID can be used as part of proof of residence when registering, often along with a document showing your current address.

Voters can call or text 844-338-8743 at any time to reach VoteRiders Voter ID Helpline

questions.q: What is the deadline to register to vote in Minnesota?
questions.a:
- Online registration deadline: 21 days before Election Day
- Register by mail deadline: Received 21 days before Election Day
- In-person registration deadline: Election Day

questions.q: How can I register to vote in Minnesota?
questions.a:
Election Day registration is available in Minnesota. However, it is encouraged that you register before Election Day. Here are your options:

- Register online (https://www.sos.state.mn.us/elections-voting/register-to-vote/register-online/)
- Register on paper (https://www.sos.state.mn.us/elections-voting/register-to-vote/register-on-paper/)
- Register on Election Day (https://www.sos.state.mn.us/elections-voting/register-to-vote/register-on-election-day/)

questions.q: Does Minnesota have Automatic Voter Registration?
questions.a:
Yes, Minnesota has automatic voter registration for eligible individuals when they apply for a driver's license, instruction permit, state ID card, or provide citizenship confirmation at the Department of Public Safety or another participating state agency.

Existing registered voters will have their information updated to reflect any changes in address or name provided to the agency, and new or updated registrants will receive a postcard offering the option to decline their new registration or registration change.

questions.q: How can I check my voter registration status?
questions.a: You can verify your voter registration status using Minnesota’s voter information tool. (https://mnvotes.sos.mn.gov/voterstatuscheck/index)

questions.q: Does Minnesota have online voter registration?
questions.a: Yes! Use our online registration tool (https://www.vote411.org/register) to complete your application

questions.q: Is same-day voter registration available in Minnesota?
questions.a: Yes, Minnesota has same-day voter registration.

questions.q: Can I pre-register to vote?
questions.a: Yes, you can pre-register to vote if you are 16 or 17 years old.

questions.q: Who is eligible to register in Minnesota?
questions.a: Check if you’re eligible to register here (https://www.vote411.org/minnesota#eligibility-requirements).

questions.q: What types of voting machines does Minnesota use?
questions.a: The voting systems used in Minnesota are Optical Scan, Paper Ballots, and Direct Recording Electronic (DRE).

questions.q: What is optical scan voting?
questions.a:
With optical scan voting, you will receive a card or sheet of paper, which you take over to a private table or booth. The card has the names of the various candidates and ballot measures printed on it.

- With a pen or pencil, you fill in a little box, circle, or space between two arrows.
- When you are finished filling out all the cards, you may bring the cards over to a ballot box, where poll workers will show you how to put the cards in the box.
- Or in some places, you may feed the completed cards or papers into a computer device that checks your card or paper right there at the polling place to make sure you have voted the way you want to and counts the votes.

questions.q: What are paper ballots?
questions.a:
Paper ballots are one of the oldest ways of voting in America.

When you come to the polling place, you will get a paper ballot from the poll worker. You take it to the voting booth, and use a pen or pencil to mark a box next to your candidate and issue choices. You then drop the marked ballot into a sealed ballot box.

questions.q: What is Direct Recording Electronic Voting?
questions.a:
Direct Recording Electronic (DRE) is the newest system in use in the U.S. All the information about who and what you are voting for is on an electronic screen like a TV or computer screen.

There are many variations of DREs because many companies are inventing new ones, and many cities, counties, and states are trying them out.

- Usually, after you have signed in, the poll workers will give you a card that you slide into a device to start your voting session.
- Some of these devices will show all candidates and ballot choices on one big screen. Often, with these big screen devices you push a button next to the name of the candidate you want to vote for (or yes or no on a ballot measure).
- On other DREs, the screen is set up to show pages. There will probably be one thing on which to vote on each screen or page. For example, on one screen or page, you might vote for the president. Then you might move to the next page to vote for a senator. Often these small-screen devices have a touch screen, where you touch the screen next to the name of the person you want to vote for.
- Other devices have a keypad, and some have a keyboard, so you can write in the name of someone you want to vote for.
- You let the system know you are finished voting by pushing a button, touching the screen or entering something on a keypad.

You can learn more about voting systems by checking out the Elections Assistance Commission's (EAC) resource.  (https://www.eac.gov/voting-equipment/system-certification-process)

questions.q: Campaign Finance Information
questions.a: For information on federal campaign contributions, please visit Open Secrets (http://www.opensecrets.org).

questions.q: Candidate and Ballot Measure Information
questions.a: Information on local, state and federal candidates and ballot measures may be available here (https://www.vote411.org/ballot#.UFoDEFHh-Sp).

questions.q: Election Dates
questions.a:
The next election date can be found here https://www.vote411.org/minnesota.

To find out information about local elections contact your local League of Women Voters or contact your local Board of Elections (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm).

questions.q: Election Day Voting Hours
questions.a: Most polling places are open from 7:00 am to 8:00 pm. Please contact your county auditor, county election office, or township clerk (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm) for details.

questions.q: Overseas and Military Voters
questions.a:
You are a Military or Overseas voter if you are in uniformed services, living overseas OR a spouse or dependent of a uniformed services voter. To get registered and vote, you can utilize Overseas Vote Foundation. (https://www.overseasvotefoundation.org/about-contact)

If you have additional questions about elections and voting overseas you can use our state specific elections official directory or contact the Overseas Vote Foundation. (https://www.overseasvotefoundation.org/about-contact)

questions.q: Polling Place Locations
questions.a:
You can find your polling place by utilizing your state resource (http://pollfinder.sos.state.mn.us/).

If you have further questions on your polling place location, please contact your county auditor, county election office, or township clerk (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm).

questions.q: Primary Election Process
questions.a:
Minnesota is an “open primary” state. You can choose the party’s ballot you wish to vote. This decision does not register you with that party and it is a private decision.

If you have any questions about your state’s primary election, please contact your local election officials (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm).

questions.q: Verify Voter Registration
questions.a:
To verify your voter registration status

  click here!  (https://mnvotes.sos.state.mn.us/VoterStatus.aspx)

questions.q: Vote by Mail
questions.a:
Some jurisdictions in Minnesota hold elections by mail instead of voting at polling places. All non-metropolitan townships and cities with less than 400 registered voters located outside of the Minneapolis/St. Paul seven-county metropolitan area can choose to hold elections by mail. If you are an active registered voter in a mail ballot precinct, you will be sent a mail ballot to your residence without having to complete an absentee ballot application.

Other options for mail ballot precinct voters on Election Day:

Mail ballot voters on Election Day from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. can:

- Return their voted mail ballot in-person to their county elections office
- Have someone else return their voted mail ballot to their county elections office (limit of three others’ ballots can be returned).
- Take their unvoted ballot packet to their county election office, vote it, and turn it in.
- Go to their county election office and inform them that your mail ballot was spoiled, lost, thrown away, etc. and:

  - Have a replacement ballot issued
  - Vote the replacement ballot
  - Turn it in
- Vote an absentee ballot because they are currently not an “active” registered voter on Election Day

For more information on mail ballot precincts click here (https://www.sos.state.mn.us/elections-voting/how-elections-work/mail-ballot-precincts/).
